title: Anthropic Lab Solves First Protein Vault Structure From Bacteriophage
summary:
A research team using the Claude AI assistant has discovered that barrel-shaped protein structures known as "vaults," once thought to exist only in complex organisms, also assemble in bacteria and the viruses that infect them. Using a method led by biochemist Januka Athukoralage, the biologists at Anthropic identified the first 3D structure of a vault particle from a bacteriophage and found similar proteins in 8 different bacterial species. The team found that these structures are larger than ribosomes and demonstrated that they could use the AI to expand the size of the protein walls by engineering additional repeats.

The project aimed to uncover the biological function of these particles, which were first discovered in human cells in 1986 but remain a mystery. While Anthropic found the AI cut particle isolation time from 3 days to 90 minutes and delivered a structural model in 34 hours, the tool made errors during the process. The biology team reported that Claude omitted a standard cryo-EM step and incorrectly blended a protein map with its mirror image, necessitating corrections from the company’s machine learning researchers.

selectedTweets.text:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

selectedTweets.text:
Thrilled to share new work from our experimental biology lab at @AnthropicAI. Led by world-class biochemist Januka Athukoralage, we built a rapid method for the isolation and structural characterization of vaults. It turns out these massive structures are not just found in eukaryotic cells, but also in prokaryotes and even phages. We solve the structure of one of these phage vaults, and then demonstrate we can engineer additional repeats into the wall to make it bigger.

One thing I can't get over about these vaults. They seem to be widespread across life - we assembled them from 8 different bacteria and bacteriophages. But they are just so massive - bigger than ribosomes, AAV, and even some phage capsids. Why devote so much energy to making these huge complexes? They have to be doing something useful - I hope that's the question that gets answered next. 

Amazing collaboration with @PeterHYoon, @amirshanehsaz, @eric_kabrams, and @mgdurrant! Grateful to our team for making Claude an amazing labmate and to Anthropic for supporting this type of work on fundamental biology. 

Natural mysteries abound - let's get to solving them!

Blog: https://t.co/O6VtahFIvo 

Technical report: https://t.co/erue23SFWl
